item.title: Self-Care 2.0: Saying “No” and Setting Limits
item.description:
Stress

Self-Care 2.0: Saying “No” and Setting Limits

Sometimes the best way to care for yourself is to set clear boundaries.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • What we consciously choose not to do can be a powerful form of self-care.
  • The best form of self-care might be where you draw the line and say "no."
  • Setting boundaries with people and situations is an important part of caring for yourself.

Sometimes it is the things we choose not to do that can have a powerful impact on our lives. It is certainly true when it comes to self-care. Think about how it feels when you engage in something that exhausts you and you realize that you had the option of opting out. It can be as simple as declining an outing with a friend because you prefer time alone to unwind. Oftentimes the best form of self-care is where you draw the line and say “no.”

Caring about ourselves is never optional. Self-care is about what we do to support ourselves in the context of the stressors of everyday life. It is how we care for ourselves in ways that help us to reset from the demands of daily living. A recent study compared the stress-reducing effects of self-care versus learning to improve coping skills (Riegel et al., 2024). The study concluded that self-care was more effective in reducing stress and improving mental health. Self-care has a significant impact on overall well-being, and the practice of self-care deserves time and attention.

What usually comes to mind when we think of self-care is a spa day, listening to favorite music, or ordering takeout when you don’t feel like cooking. Although self-care is largely about what you do for yourself, it is equally important to take inventory of things in your life that you might consider eliminating. How often do we automatically engage in pursuits that, in hindsight, are stressful and unnecessary? Are there activities that we believe are obligatory but are not? At times, we do things that are not in our best interest when we believe we have no choice. There are always things that we must do, but there are also many situations where we have choices. Exercising those choices is sometimes the best form of self-care.

Learning to set healthy boundaries with people and situations is an important part of caring for yourself. Self-care requires thoughtful examination and deciding whether an activity or a relationship might cause distress. In some instances, self-care is setting necessary limits.

9 Practical Applications of Self-Care

The following are nine practical applications of self-care involving opting out and setting limits.

  1. Choosing not to go out when you prefer to stay in. Sometimes it is more important to act on your preference instead of trying to meet the expectations of others.
  2. Declining social invitations that will surely drain your energy. Sometimes it is necessary to conserve your energy instead of doing things that will exhaust you, physically and/or mentally.
  3. Choosing not to answer a predictably upsetting phone call. Sometimes it's important to set a boundary that honors your emotional limits at that moment. There will be opportunities to speak later.
  4. Turning off the evening news. Sometimes protecting your peace of mind is more important than being informed at that moment.
  5. Eliminating open-ended doomscrolling. Sometimes social media can be agitating. At those times, setting a boundary is an important part of self-care.
  6. Choosing not to spend time with an ill-tempered acquaintance. Sometimes being around certain people can be stressful and not restorative.
  7. Not eating food that tastes good now but will cause indigestion later. Sometimes respecting the limits of your body means being careful about what you eat and how it will affect you.
  8. Choosing not to wear uncomfortable clothing. Sometimes self-care is preempting physical discomfort.
  9. Choosing not to engage in a needless argument. Sometimes it is important to avoid introducing needless stress into your relationships, especially for things that don't really matter.

Caring for yourself might be as simple as giving yourself permission to say “no” and rethinking what does not effectively meet your needs. What we consciously choose not to do can be a powerful form of self-care.

item.title: The Origins of Narcissism
item.description:
Narcissism

The Origins of Narcissism

The origins of narcissism lie in a person's attachment style.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Understanding the origins of narcissism allows us to try and prevent it.
  • A primary attachment figure's continuous type of response or non-response determines the attachment style.
  • An insecure attachment style is a predictor of narcissism in adulthood.

Everyone has narcissistic tendencies, yet if these tendencies are extreme, they can prevent a person from being an emotionally safe person in a close relationship, meaning it is difficult for them to perspective-take, have empathy in place of sympathy, be truly accountable, look in the mirror, and be aware of how their words and actions impact loved ones. They may also have a victim stance which protects them from having to take accountability because they rewrite history and place themselves as the “victim” in any scenario and you as the “villain.” This may lead them to unfairly attack and mischaracterize you. Yet, when all the smoke disappears, they move on like nothing ever happened.

You suffer significantly, and they have no idea that they are continually hurting you because they distort things to view themselves as innocent. However, their lack of self-awareness and distortions cannot excuse their emotional mistreatment of others. Nor can you continue to enable them at your cost. It is an impossible situation.

However, if people are educated on the origins of narcissism, where it starts, and how it happens, they can identify ways to protect themselves. More importantly, as a culture, we can try to prevent it from happening in the first place.

The Link Between Insecure Attachment and Narcissism

The research indicates that narcissism stems from an insecure attachment style. This does not mean that if you feel insecure in a relationship that you automatically have an insecure attachment style. For example, a narcissist exploits your insecurities by being hot and cold, amongst other things. And, in many cases, if you are aware of your insecurities and grapple with them daily, you may be strong enough to handle your flaws. You take responsibility for them instead of projecting them onto others. This is a sign of a secure attachment style.

So, let’s start at the very beginning. Barring significant impairment, all infants enter this world neurologically programmed to attach. Cross culturally, all infants cry, grope, make eye contact, smile, babble, root, and routinely exhibit a preference for their primary caregiver. When the primary caregiver is emotionally attuned, they pick up on the baby’s signals, and consistently respond with empathy, meaning they routinely meet the baby’s needs and regularly comfort the baby in times of distress. Delighting in the young child’s accomplishments and mirroring the child during play are also important parental tasks that help solidify a secure attachment between the primary attachment figure and baby. The baby develops trust in the caregiver and feels loved. The result is a healthy sense of self, which can produce an adult who is strong enough to handle their flaws, have empathy, be accountable, and take a loved one’s perspective to try to understand them better, even if they have a differing feeling or opinion.

Alternatively, when a primary caregiver is self-absorbed and emotionally unavailable, they miss the infant’s cries for help and tend to perceive the infant as a burden… almost as if the baby’s needs are an imposition. Because they view the infant as someone that is trying to hinder them, they feel it is OK to ignore, dismiss, and admonish the baby for having needs.

How Chronic Neglect Shapes Insecure (Avoidant) Attachment

If the infant, despite their signals of distress, is routinely ignored for lengthy periods of time on a long-term basis, they experience significant emotional pain. Their trust in their caregiver begins to wane. If this continues for most of their first two years, the infant’s belief in their attachment figure may dissipate and they withdraw. They stop signaling for help because the hurt intensifies when they are ignored and it can feel unbearable. They learn that they can only count on themselves. Being vulnerable, trusting, having empathy for others, and being accountable are next to impossible because they rarely experienced it in their attachment relationship. They tend to fold into themselves and focus on protecting themselves from any further pain. This defensiveness and egocentrism may begin to take hold to protect a sense of self that is so fragile that, in adulthood, they may always need to have the upper hand in their relationships, even if it means emotionally mistreating a partner to get it. This is often referred to as an insecure (avoidant) attachment style.

Almost as detrimental is the primary attachment figure who is erratic and unpredictable in their responses to the baby. Sometimes they offer comfort and sometimes they neglect the infant. The small child cannot trust that the caretaker will help them because this attachment figure has been egregiously inconsistent for long stretches of time. Thus, the child cannot be vulnerable and signal for help because they do not know if they will be soothed or rejected. The conflict is so intense that they cannot chance it. They resort to continuous and epic temper tantrums and oppositional behaviors to force their attachment figure to remain close, and to control them. The child prefers control over closeness because their caregiver has been too unreliable. They need to control an attachment figure because the bond is too flimsy. This often leads to emotionally controlling behaviors in adulthood and is frequently referred to as an insecure (disorganized) attachment style.

The research also shows that an insecure attachment style, whether it be avoidant or disorganized, is the predictor of narcissism in adulthood. Conversely, a secure attachment style is the predictor of emotional intelligence in adulthood. These links seem to be incredibly important concepts these days.
